prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All right, I admit it: It was just a dream I had last night. I was trudging along a muddy path in a column of downcast men on the blackened outskirts of New York, the twilight dingy and ruined, the future without hope as we marched along in our soiled, proletarian rags. To my left was Mayakovsky, head shaved, and next to him his friend with gray beard and dark cap. "You've got to admit," Mayakovsky was saying, "that this is a pretty good way to write a poem." "Yes," I said, "the momentum is sustained by our walking forward, the desolate landscape seeps into every word, and you're free to say anything you want." "That's because we're inside the poem," he said, "not outside." Puddles of oily water gleamed dully beneath the low clouds. "That's why my poems were so big: there's more room inside." The hard line of his jaw flexed and the men dispersed. I followed his friend behind a wall to hear the poem go on in the lecture the friend was giving on history, but no, the real poem had finished. I went back to the spot where the poem had finished. Vladimir had left the poem.

Fine, I’ll confess: it was only a dream from last night. I found myself slogging down a mud-covered track, part of a file of dispirited men, somewhere on the charred edge of New York. The evening light was grimy and wrecked, and there seemed to be no future at all as we moved forward in our filthy working-class scraps of clothing.

On my left walked Mayakovsky, his head shaved. Beside him was his companion, a man with a gray beard and a dark cap.

“You have to acknowledge,” Mayakovsky said, “this is a fairly effective method for composing a poem.”

“It is,” I answered. “Our forward motion keeps the energy going, the bleak scenery works its way into every line, and you can say whatever you like.”

“That’s because we are within the poem,” he replied, “rather than observing it from the outside.”

Under the low clouds, slick puddles shone faintly with oily water.

“That’s why my poems were so large,” he added. “There was more space inside them.”

His firm jaw tightened, and the group of men scattered. I followed his friend around behind a wall, hoping to hear the poem continue in the history lecture the friend was delivering. But it did not; the actual poem had already ended.

I returned to the place where it had come to a close. Vladimir had gone out of the poem.
outputs.L3:
The speaker recalls a dream in which he was walking through the ruined outskirts of New York with a group of downcast men. The landscape around them was bleak and hopeless, marked by destruction and emptiness. As they moved through this desolate place, the journey itself seemed to carry the weight of despair, as though the city’s broken edges reflected the inner condition of the people passing through it.

In the dream, Mayakovsky appears and offers a striking insight: walking through such a grim and devastated landscape can itself be a powerful way to write a poem. The act of moving through the ruins is not separate from poetry, but becomes part of its creation. The setting, the motion, and the emotional atmosphere all contribute to the poem’s force.

The speaker and Mayakovsky then reflect on what it means to be “inside the poem.” From within the poem, its meaning is not imposed from outside; instead, it is shaped by the poem’s own movement, its surroundings, and its sense of freedom. The poem becomes a space one inhabits, rather than merely a set of lines on a page. To be inside it is to experience how its direction, landscape, and possibilities determine what it can say.

Mayakovsky explains that his own poems were large because there was “more room inside” them. Their size was not only a matter of length or ambition, but of inner spaciousness. They could contain movement, struggle, history, voices, cities, and emotional intensity. Their greatness came from the freedom and breadth of the world they opened within themselves.

By the end of the dream, the speaker comes to a quiet realization: the true poem has already ended. The experience of walking, listening, and understanding has completed itself. Vladimir Mayakovsky has left the poem, and with his departure the dream’s poetic space closes as well. What remains is the speaker’s awareness that the poem was not something still to be written, but something that had already happened.
outputs.L4:
Poetry can sometimes feel larger than the space it occupies on the page. A few lines may open into an entire world, not because they explain that world in detail, but because they draw the reader into its movement, weather, pressure, and mood. The experience is not simply one of understanding what a poem “means.” It is closer to entering a place, walking through it, and feeling its atmosphere gather around you.

This sense of immersion is suggested through a dreamlike encounter with Mayakovsky. The speaker seems to find himself on a bleak march through a ruined landscape, moving beside or in the presence of the poet. The scene is harsh and desolate: the world appears broken, exhausted, and stripped of comfort. Yet the march continues. What matters is not only the scenery, but the sensation of being carried forward through it. The poem becomes an environment of motion, as if its rhythm, images, and voice are all part of the same physical experience.

Mayakovsky’s presence intensifies this atmosphere. He is not treated merely as a historical figure or literary reference, but as a force within the poem’s world. His energy, his revolutionary intensity, and his association with struggle and defiance seem to haunt the landscape. The encounter feels unreal, almost like a vision or dream, but it is emotionally concrete. The speaker is not standing outside the scene, analyzing it from a distance. He is inside it, exposed to its coldness, its ruin, and its momentum.

In this way, the text suggests that poetry’s power lies in immediacy. A poem is most alive when the reader or speaker is caught within its action—when its images are not merely observed, but inhabited. The ruined landscape, the march, and the ghostly companionship of Mayakovsky all create a poetic space that feels expansive because it is experienced from within. The poem does not simply describe desolation; it makes desolation something the reader passes through.

The conclusion, then, is that true poetic experience depends on remaining inside that lived motion and atmosphere. Once the reader steps back and treats the poem only as an object to be explained, something essential is lost. Analysis may clarify structure or meaning, but it can also mark the end of the poem’s immediate life. The deepest power of poetry exists in the moment of immersion, when language becomes a world and the reader moves through it as if through weather, memory, or dream.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal first-person prose poem about dreaming you are walking through a ruined New York with Vladimir Mayakovsky, discussing how being “inside the poem” changes the way poetry works.
counterfactuals.output:
I dream I am walking through New York after the future has finished chewing it.

The avenues lie open like broken rulers. The traffic lights blink red to no one, green to ghosts, yellow to the rain that falls upward from the manholes. A ferry, half-sunk in the middle of Broadway, leans against the Flatiron Building as if exhausted by its own metaphor. In Times Square, the advertisements have lost their products and now sell only verbs: **BURN**, **REMEMBER**, **BECOME**, **HURRY**.

Beside me strides Vladimir Mayakovsky, enormous in his yellow blouse, his head brushing the low clouds. He carries a cigarette like a small industrial chimney and points at the ruins with the impatience of a man correcting bad punctuation.

“Your city,” he says, “has finally become readable.”

I tell him it was always readable, just written in money.

He laughs so loudly that pigeons pour out of the windows of the Chrysler Building, each one wearing a little soldier’s cap. “Money is only a rhyme that forgot it was a wound.”

We walk through the shell of a bank where vines have grown over the marble counters. Behind the glass, the old tellers sit as skeletons, still counting invisible withdrawals. Mayakovsky leans down and whispers into a deposit slip, and it blossoms into a red carnation.

I say, “When you are outside a poem, you can admire its machinery. The line breaks, the engines, the smoke. But inside the poem—”

“Inside,” he interrupts, “the machinery admires you.”

And suddenly the street tilts. The sidewalks become stanzas. The ruined skyscrapers arrange themselves into columns, then refuse to stay arranged. Every window is an eye, every eye a vowel. My footsteps begin to alter the meter of the city: when I hesitate, the Hudson pauses; when I breathe, the subway tunnels exhale hot iron beneath us.

Mayakovsky takes my arm. “You see? Outside the poem, poetry is an object. A monument. A dead lion in a museum. Inside the poem, it is weather. It gets into your coat. It changes the temperature of your blood.”

We pass Central Park, which has swollen into a jungle. The statues have climbed down from their pedestals and are drinking from the reservoir. Walt Whitman, made entirely of leaves, is asleep under a shattered arch, his beard full of sparrows. The moon hangs low over Harlem like a cracked plate of milk.

“But if I am inside the poem,” I ask, “who is writing?”

Mayakovsky stops in the middle of Fifth Avenue. Around us, the buildings bend closer to listen. He looks at me with those furnace eyes, those eyes that have argued with revolution, love, death, paper.

“Not who,” he says. “What.”

A siren answers from somewhere under the earth.

“The poem writes with pressure,” he says. “With hunger. With the falling brick, the unpaid bill, the kiss that arrives too late. The poet is not the owner of the poem. The poet is the door it kicks open.”

At that, every door in New York flies from its hinges. Doors from apartments, hospitals, theaters, prisons, delis, childhood bedrooms, doors I had forgotten I had closed. They whirl above us in a great wooden migration, darkening the sky.

I feel my body becoming less certain. My hands blur into commas. My ribs ring like typewriter keys. I understand then that to be inside the poem is to lose the safe distance from beauty. Nothing symbolizes anything because everything is already burning with itself. A bridge is not like a longing; the bridge longs. A tower is not like a spine; the tower aches. The dead do not stand for memory; they ask for coffee, directions, revenge.

Mayakovsky smiles as if I have finally learned the alphabet by being struck with it.

“Yes,” he says. “Now poetry is not description. It is participation.”

We climb the Empire State Building by walking up its shadow. At the top, the whole ruined city lies below us, glittering with broken glass and stubborn rivers. Brooklyn floats loose like a ship cut from its moorings. The Statue of Liberty has set down her torch and is warming both hands over its flame.

Mayakovsky opens his coat. Inside it, instead of a lining, there is a storm of unfinished lines, barricades, lovers, factories, stars. He offers me one.

I take it. It wriggles in my palm like a live wire.

“Careful,” he says. “A line is not a leash. It is a fuse.”

Below us, New York begins to rebuild itself incorrectly. The libraries grow roots. The police stations turn into bakeries. The stock exchange fills with horses. In the windows of the ruined towers, people made of light lean out and shout my name, but each shout changes me slightly, until my name is no longer a label but a ladder.

I ask Mayakovsky if waking will end the poem.

He flicks his cigarette into the dawn, and the dawn catches fire.

“Waking,” he says, “is only another stanza with worse lighting.”

Then he steps off the building and does not fall. He walks outward into the air as if crossing an avenue, his boots striking invisible syllables. I follow because the poem has no outside anymore, because even fear has become a form of rhythm, because far below, the ruined city is chanting in steam and rust and green leaves:

You are not reading this.

You are being read.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short literary vignette in the style of a bleak modernist dream journal, featuring Mayakovsky as a companion on a muddy march through a dystopian landscape.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the road had no beginning, only mud remembering boots.

Mayakovsky walked beside me in a yellow scarf, enormous and tired, his pockets full of broken proclamations. Now and then he took one out, unfolded it, and found it blank from the rain. He laughed without sound. Ahead, the city leaned on the horizon like a burned-out factory whistle, all ribs and smokestacks, exhaling crows.

We marched with others, though their faces had been rubbed smooth by sleep. A woman carried a door on her back. A child dragged a clock whose hands kept pointing downward. No one spoke; speech had been requisitioned in the night.

“Comrade,” Mayakovsky said, “even the puddles have learned to reflect only orders.”

I looked down. In the brown water my face wore a soldier’s cap. His wore a window nailed shut.

The mud deepened. It entered our boots, then our thoughts. Each step made a wet bureaucratic sound, as if the earth were stamping forms in triplicate. Somewhere beyond the fog, loudspeakers recited the names of extinct flowers.

By evening we reached a field of black telegraph poles. Their wires sagged like old nerves. Mayakovsky stopped, raised his fist toward the colorless sky, and opened his mouth to shout a poem large enough to wake the dead.

Only rain came out.

We continued marching after that, because in the dream there was no other verb.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a strange, melancholic paragraph where the narrator admits a political apocalypse scene was only a dream, then meets Mayakovsky and talks with him about the mechanics of poetry.
counterfactuals.output: In the morning I had to admit the parliament of crows, the ministers with ash in their mouths, the red flags burning like wet leaves over the drowned avenues, had only been a dream—no regime had fallen in the night except the small tyrannies of my sleep—and yet the day felt evacuated, as if history had packed its suitcases and left by the service stairs. I found Mayakovsky waiting under a broken clock, enormous and tired, tapping cigarette ash into a puddle that reflected no sky. “You confused thunder with argument,” he said, not unkindly. I asked him how a poem could survive when every word seemed requisitioned by slogans, and he shrugged his great shoulders: “By engineering its own weather. Line breaks are hinges, rhythm is a factory belt, metaphor is the sabotage that makes the machine reveal its soul.” We walked past shuttered kiosks and leafless trees while he explained that poetry was not escape from politics but pressure applied to language until it confessed its hidden architecture; then he grew transparent in the drizzle, leaving me with the terrible peace of waking, and a sentence in my pocket ticking like a bomb that had forgotten what it meant to destroy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an AI-generated passage that sounds like a lost prose poem: ruined city outskirts, proletarian marchers, oily puddles, Mayakovsky explaining why his poems were so large, and an ending where he leaves the poem.
counterfactuals.output:
At the outskirts of the ruined city, where the last tramline ended in a snarl of wire and nettles, the workers came marching under banners darkened by rain. Their boots struck the broken road without music. In the oily puddles the clouds lay face-down, iridescent and defeated, as if the sky itself had been spilled from a barrel and left to rot among brick dust, cabbage leaves, and bolts of red cloth.

Mayakovsky stood on a heap of masonry with his coat open to the wind. He was too tall for the street and too loud for the twilight. When someone asked him why his poems were so large, he pointed not to his chest, not to the heavens, but to the marchers passing below.

“Because,” he said, “a small poem cannot carry a factory. A small poem cannot lift a bridge, cannot house a widow, cannot shout over artillery, cannot make room for a thousand wet boots coming home at dawn. I wrote them large because the century was large—large in hunger, large in lies, large in its mouth. I had to build lines with doors in them.”

The puddles trembled. The banners went on. In the distance the city smoked like a blackened samovar, and every window was an eye that had forgotten how to close.

Mayakovsky climbed down from the rubble. He brushed the dust from his sleeves, though more fell at once. Then, without farewell, he walked past the last marching column, past the puddles holding their spoiled rainbows, past the sentence that had been waiting to finish him.

At the margin of the page he paused, turned sideways, and stepped out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal microfiction piece in first person about being trapped inside a poem with Mayakovsky on the blackened outskirts of New York, blending dream logic, literary criticism, and post-revolutionary despair.
counterfactuals.output:
I woke in the margin, where the snow had been erased and the factories were still smoking their bad metaphors.

Mayakovsky stood beside me on the blackened outskirts of New York, enormous as a headline, his yellow blouse flickering like a warning lamp in the ash. Beyond us, Manhattan rose on stilts of bone and advertising, its windows punched out, its bridges sagging like tired arguments. Every street sign had been revised by an invisible editor: **BROADWAY** became **BREADWAY**, **WALL STREET** became **WAIL STREET**, and the Hudson moved backward, carrying dead ferries toward the womb of Europe.

“We are trapped inside a poem,” I said.

“Naturally,” Mayakovsky replied, lighting a cigarette from the burning moon. “Where else would they put men who believed in the future?”

The poem had no exit, only enjambments. Each time I ran toward the last line, the stanza broke and I fell into another image: a room full of red telephones ringing under water; a horse wearing spectacles, lecturing on commodity fetishism; Lenin’s portrait dissolving into a billboard for soap. The rhyme scheme limped after us like a wounded dog.

Mayakovsky kicked at the meter. “Bad construction,” he said. “Too much symbolism. Not enough steel.”

“But the steel rusted,” I told him. “The workers are ghosts. The revolution has become a museum gift shop.”

He stared at the skyline, where skyscrapers leaned together like conspirators. In their lit offices, tiny clerks stamped **FAILURE** on clouds. Somewhere inside the poem, a critic cleared his throat and accused us of excessive pathos.

Mayakovsky laughed, but the laugh came out as broken glass. “Critics always arrive after the collapse,” he said. “They mistake rubble for architecture.”

We walked until the page curled upward at the edge of Queens. There the suburbs were charred, the lawns black, the mailboxes full of unsent manifestos. I found a door drawn in ink on the air. I opened it and saw only more poem: ladders made of exclamation points, a sun nailed to a tenement wall, my own body described in the third person.

“Can we escape?” I asked.

Mayakovsky placed his vast hand on my shoulder. His eyes were two exhausted factories.

“No,” he said. “But we can revise the prison.”

So we began crossing out the darkness with our fingers. Underneath it was more darkness, but warmer, almost human.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
